take: The market’s core driver remains the Strait of Hormuz disruption, with the EIA now seeing 600,000 bpd of Middle East supply still offline by end-2027, a longer-than-expected closure that keeps the geopolitical risk premium firmly embedded in crude and products. Refinery attacks on Russian and Saudi facilities are deepening the global diesel supply crunch, with prices surging earlier this week as the market grapples with an already out-of-balance fuel system. On the freight side, the threat of Russian seizures of EU ships and the widening drone campaign against Libya’s Zawiya oil hub are forcing rerouting and raising war risk premiums, with Skuld cancelling Red Sea cover from August 16 and the IMO urging reassessment of transit risks. Positioning is cautious, with oil rangebound on suspicions that a US/Iran peace deal is unfeasible, whilst the IEA’s contraction call for demand this year caps upside and keeps speculative length in check. Watch for any further escalation in the Strait of Hormuz or Black Sea grain terminals over the next 24 hours, as a fresh attack could trigger a sharp repricing of both crude and bunker fuel differentials.
